paragraphs: 12 Some time later, Joseph’s brothers had gone to pasture their father’s flocks near Shechem. 13 Israel said to him, “Are not your brothers pasturing the flocks at Shechem? Get ready; I am sending you to them.” “I am ready,” Joseph replied.

14 Then Israel told him, “Go now and see how your brothers and the flocks are faring, and bring word back to me.” So he sent him off from the Valley of Hebron. And when Joseph arrived in Shechem, 15 a man found him wandering in the field and asked, “What are you looking for?”
16 “I am looking for my brothers,” Joseph replied. “Can you please tell me where they are pasturing their flocks?”
17 “They have moved on from here,” the man answered. “I heard them say, ‘Let us go to Dothan.’” So Joseph set out after his brothers and found them at Dothan.

18 Now Joseph’s brothers saw him in the distance, and before he arrived, they plotted to kill him. 19 “Here comes that dreamer!” they said to one another. 20 “Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits. We can say that a vicious animal has devoured him. Then we shall see what becomes of his dreams!”

21 When Reuben heard this, he tried to rescue Joseph from their hands. “Let us not take his life,” he said. 22 “Do not shed his blood. Throw him into this pit in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him.” Reuben said this so that he could rescue Joseph from their hands and return him to his father.

23 So when Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his robe—the robe of many colors he was wearing— 24 and they took him and threw him into the pit. Now the pit was empty, with no water in it.
25 And as they sat down to eat a meal, they looked up and saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead. Their camels were carrying spices, balm, and myrrh on their way down to Egypt.

26 Then Judah said to his brothers, “What profit will we gain if we kill our brother and cover up his blood? 27 Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites and not lay a hand on him; for he is our brother, our own flesh.” And they agreed. 28 So when the Midianite traders passed by, his brothers pulled Joseph out of the pit and sold him for twenty shekels of silver to the Ishmaelites, who took him to Egypt.
29 When Reuben returned to the pit and saw that Joseph was not there, he tore his clothes, 30 returned to his brothers, and said, “The boy is gone! What am I going to do?”

context_lines: Jacob sends Joseph to check on his brothers and the flocks near Shechem. After a man directs him to Dothan, Joseph finds them. They see him coming and plan to kill him, dispose of his body, and blame a wild animal. Their reference to his dreams makes their hostility to his anticipated authority explicit.

Reuben intervenes, urging them to put Joseph in a pit without shedding his blood. The narrator tells us his intention is to rescue Joseph and return him to their father. The brothers strip off the distinctive robe and throw Joseph into an empty pit, then sit down to eat. [Genesis 42:21](https://biblehub.com/bsb/genesis/42.htm) later recalls that they heard his distress and pleas but would not listen.

When traders traveling toward Egypt appear, Judah proposes selling Joseph instead of killing him. The brothers agree and sell him for twenty shekels of silver. Joseph's life is spared, but he is still betrayed and carried away as a slave. Reuben returns to the pit, finds him gone, and tears his clothes in distress.

The passage uses both Ishmaelite and Midianite descriptions for the traders. Its immediate focus is the brothers' wrongdoing and Joseph's removal to Egypt. Their attempt to prevent his dreams from coming true sets him on the road to the place where his later authority will emerge.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly read this as a grave betrayal that God will nevertheless turn toward the family's preservation. [Wesley's notes on Genesis 37:18–26](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/) emphasize both the brothers' deliberate wrongdoing and the purpose that emerges beyond their intentions. The [Catholic Catechism, paragraph 312](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_one/section_two/chapter_one/article_1/paragraph_4_the_creator.html), also uses Joseph's story to explain that God can bring good from human evil without making the evil itself good.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
god_plan_lines: [Acts 7:9–10](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/7.htm) directly recalls this event: the patriarchs' jealousy leads them to sell Joseph, but God is with him and eventually raises him to authority in Egypt. Stephen later confronts his own hearers over their rejection of the Righteous One in Acts 7:51–53. His speech shows that rejection by people does not mean rejection by God.

The beloved son sent to his brothers and met with a plot against his life also offers a meaningful parallel to Christ's rejection, noted in [Wesley's commentary on Genesis 37:21](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/). The connection concerns the pattern of rejection followed by God's saving work. Joseph's suffering will help preserve his family; Christ's saving work reaches further, dealing with sin itself. God's ability to bring good does not excuse the people who betray either of them.
